To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the three dependent measures of choice, time allocation and response rate yielded similar gradients of generalization, and that changes in the relative density of reinforcement for the two responses produced shifts in the location of the gradients, but had little effect on their shape.

the three measures we used to assess generalization yielded gradients of similar shape and slope that were sensitive to changes in the contingencies of differential reinforcement, and that choice, time allocation and response rate were differentially affected by changes in reinforcement density.
choice, time allocation and response rate all generalize to the stimulus continuum, and that choice generalizes more than time allocation and response rates.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of relative reinforcement density on the stimulus generalization gradients of choice, time allocation and response rate.
the relation between choice, time allocation and response rate in a generalization paradigm, in which the two stimuli were defined by differences in noise intensity.
the relation between choice and response rate, with the role of reinforcement in shaping these two measures, and with the relation between response rate and choice in generalization.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results of this experiment are consistent with the view that choice, time allocation and response rate are controlled by the same variables.

the results of this experiment support the notion that choice and rate processes are controlled by different contingencies of reinforcement, but that choice is more sensitive to changes than rate, at least when measured by the methods used here.

the effects of reinforcement on choice, time allocation (time allocation in the sense of the time spent in a component initiated by a given key), and response rate are all different, but all are related to one another.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
choice and time allocation are controlled by stimulus intensity, while response rate is controlled by relative reinforcement density.
the choice, time allocation and momentary response rate gradients were all sigmoidal and that the location of these gradients was affected by the relative reinforcement densities of the two stimuli.

choice, time allocation to components, momentary response rate, and the absolute number of responses all depend on reinforcement density, but that these measures are differentially sensitive to changes in the contingencies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the three measures of responding yielded gradients of similar shape, which were affected by reinforcement density in different ways.
the three measures of behavior we used (choice, time allocation, response rate) can provide a more detailed picture of the dynamics of stimulus generalization than any one of them alone.
choice, time allocation and response rate are not independent measures of behavior, and that all three measures should be considered when studying stimulus generalization.
